meta.name: Virality Simulator evaluation framework
meta.purpose: Tells the personas what tends to make people stop, watch and send a short video in each niche, so that feedback is specific instead of generic. It does not predict views.
how_to_use: Inject only the rules of the detected niche (plus the common criteria) into the persona prompt and the suggestions prompt.
Personas still judge as real scrollers. The rules explain what matters in the niche. A missing rule is not an automatic penalty.
Never say a sound or format is 'trending'. The simulator cannot detect that.

Suggestions must cite a persona quote from this run. They may name a rule id from this file as the reason, but must not invent numbers, tools or techniques that are not in the brief, the persona text or this file.
limitations: Sources are platform statements, platform ad-creative guides and one academic study. None of them was validated against our own reels.
TikTok and Meta guidance in this file is written for ADS and for other platforms. Applying it to organic Instagram Reels is an extrapolation.
The Guo et al. study is about minutes-long MOOC videos, not 30-second reels. Applying it to education reels is an extrapolation.
Comedy and fitness have no niche-specific source. Their rules are reasoning from the common criteria and need validation.
Meta's multipliers (1.5x, 1.7x, 2.0x...) are the platform's own correlational ad-study numbers, reported second-hand. Do not use them as weights.
Scoring weights are deliberately NOT in this file. They stay in core/config.py until they are fitted on real reels.
meta.quote_check_status: All quotes were returned by a page-fetch summarizer, not copied by a human. quote_verified is false everywhere. Open the url and check at least 5 quotes before relying on them.

claim_type_values.platform_statement: A named person at the platform said it (reported by an article).
claim_type_values.platform_guide: Platform's own creator or ad guide.
claim_type_values.inference: Our reasoning built on a cited source, not stated by the source.

sources.title: Instagram shares algorithm tips for 2025 (Social Media Today, Andrew Hutchinson)
sources.speaker: Adam Mosseri, head of Instagram (first video of a new series)
quotes: The top three signals that matter most for ranking are watch time, likes and sends.
So when looking at your insights, pay close attention to average watch time, likes per reach, and sends per reach.
Likes are slightly more important for connected content, and sends are slightly more important for unconnected content.
caveats: Comments and originality are not mentioned in this statement.
The article author's own interpretations (comments count inside watch time, carousels rank higher) are NOT Instagram statements and are not used here.

caveats: Same statement as ig_mosseri_smt, reported by a second outlet.

keep it high-quality, original and engaging from the first second.
The sweet spot for tutorials, day-in-my-life clips and most creative formats.

sources.title: YouTube demystifies the Shorts algorithm, views and answers other creator questions (TechCrunch, Sarah Perez)
sources.speaker: Todd Sherman, YouTube Shorts product lead
quotes: There are parts of the algorithm that try and find people, find creators an audience
And depending on how that goes, it may get a lot more traffic or it may taper off
paraphrased_points: A Shorts view counts only with some intent to watch, not every swipe (threshold not published).
No video length is inherently better; use what the story needs (Shorts max 60 seconds at the time).
Posting time and posting volume are not factors; quality matters more than quantity.
caveats: From 2023. Most points are the journalist's paraphrase of Sherman, only the two quotes are his words.
The test-then-expand behaviour described here is the reason Wave 1 / gate / Wave 2 is a reasonable design, but it is not proof that our simulator matches it.

sources.title: How Video Production Affects Student Engagement: An Empirical Study of MOOC Videos
sources.speaker: Philip J. Guo, Juho Kim, Rob Rubin (Learning at Scale 2014)
quotes: shorter videos are much more engaging
informal talking-head videos are more engaging
Students generally engaged more with videos where instructors spoke faster.
Khan-style tablet drawings are more engaging
even high-quality pre-recorded classroom lectures might not make for engaging online videos
caveats: Videos were minutes long and watched by enrolled students. Engagement = watch time and problem attempts, not learning.
The authors say faster speech probably reflects instructor enthusiasm, not speed itself.
Several comparisons rest on one pair of courses, so instructor and subject may confound results.

common_criteria.name: Hook
common_criteria.question_for_persona: In the first 1-3 seconds, is there a clear reason to stop scrolling (a visible result, a question, a surprise, a promise)?
look_for: Something concrete on screen in the first second
Text or speech that states the promise or setup
No slow intro, logo animation or throat-clearing
red_flags: Generic opening shot with no stated payoff
Long intro or logo before the point

common_criteria.name: Clarity
common_criteria.question_for_persona: Can a first-time viewer understand what this is and what is going on, with and without sound?
look_for: Spoken content also visible as captions or text
The visual makes sense even if the viewer misses a word
red_flags: Several ideas competing in a few seconds

common_criteria.name: Retention (watch time)
common_criteria.question_for_persona: Is there a reason to keep watching until the end (payoff, next step, progress, a promise kept)?
look_for: A payoff that arrives and is worth waiting for
Variety (cuts, angles, steps) instead of a static shot
red_flags: Payoff arrives too late or never
common_criteria.note: Instagram names watch time as a top ranking signal. YouTube says a view needs some intent to watch.

common_criteria.name: Shareability (sends) and resonance (likes)
common_criteria.question_for_persona: Would a viewer send this to a specific friend, or like it because it matches who they are?
look_for: Relatable or useful enough to send to someone
A feeling or identity the viewer recognises
red_flags: Interesting but nothing to send to anyone
Only makes sense to the creator
common_criteria.note: Mosseri says sends matter more for unconnected content (reach beyond followers) and likes more for connected content. That reach beyond followers needs sends is OUR inference.

common_criteria.name: Sound and on-screen text
common_criteria.question_for_persona: Does the video work with sound on AND with sound off? Do sound and text support each other?
look_for: Message carried by both audio and text or visuals
red_flags: Punchline or key step only in audio
Audio that clashes with the visuals
common_criteria.note: Do not claim a sound is trending. The simulator cannot detect trends.

common_criteria.name: Call to action
common_criteria.question_for_persona: Is there a natural next step (try it, send it, follow, comment), and does it feel like a natural ending?
look_for: A simple next step stated in text or voice
CTA that matches the video's promise
red_flags: No next step in a video that clearly wants one

niche_detection.how: Add a niche_category field (one of niche_category_enum) to the existing brief call, so no extra API call is needed. If the model is unsure or the video fits none, it must answer general.
niche_detection.note: The brief's free-text topic_niche stays as it is. niche_category is only used to pick rules from this file.

education.label: Education

rules.rule: Open with the question, problem or surprising fact the video will answer, in the first second, in text and speech.
One idea per video. An informal, face-to-camera explanation, or a hand-drawn or step-by-step visual, tends to hold attention better than dense slides or screen text.
rules.extrapolation_warning: Study is on minutes-long MOOC videos.

rules.rule: Keep it short and moving. Energy and enthusiasm in the speaker matter more than speaking fast. Reels of 15-60 seconds are described by Instagram as the sweet spot for tutorials.
Would a viewer send this to someone who needs the answer? Useful and specific beats general.
Spoken explanation should also appear as captions so it works with sound off.
A natural next step: save, send to a friend, or follow for the next part. Keep it short.

common_mistakes: Starts with a greeting or channel intro instead of the question

comedy.label: Comedy

rules.rule: The setup must be visible in the first second (situation, caption or character). The viewer should know what the joke is about before the punchline.
Check the joke twice: with sound on and with sound off. If the punchline only works in audio, flag it. If it works through on-screen text, sound adds less.
Punchline timing: the payoff should arrive before attention drops. A short video with one clear payoff beats a longer one with a late payoff.
Relatable humour is often sent to a specific friend ('this is you'). Judge: who would this be sent to, and why?
Reused audio or a familiar clip may be recognised by the audience. Judge whether it adds to the joke. Never claim a sound is trending.
Comedy usually needs no explicit CTA. A forced CTA can hurt the joke.

common_mistakes: Joke needs context the viewer does not have
Relies only on a borrowed template with nothing of the creator's own
comedy.evidence_note: No comedy-specific source was found. These rules are reasoning and need validation on real reels.

beauty.label: Beauty

rules.rule: Show or promise the result in the first seconds (the look, the instant effect, a before shot).
Show how the product is used, step by step, from the viewer's point of view. Application should look easy.
Before/after or side-by-side comparisons give a reason to wait for the reveal.
Would a viewer send this to a friend who wants this look or product?
Conversational, casual voice and audio that fits the mood. Add text for product names and steps so it works silently.
A simple, direct next step at the end.

common_mistakes: Steps and product names not visible as text

fitness.label: Fitness

rules.rule: Show the movement or the result, or state the promise, in the first second.
The viewer should be able to copy the move: form visible, reps or sets stated as text, one exercise or idea at a time.
A visible progression (rep count, steps, transformation reveal) gives a reason to watch to the end. Tutorials of 15-60 seconds are described by Instagram as a sweet spot.
Would a viewer send this to a gym or workout partner, or save it for later?
Many people watch with sound off. Exercise names and reps should appear as text.
A natural next step: save, send to a partner, or follow for the full routine.

common_mistakes: No text for reps or sets
Claims about results with no visible proof
fitness.evidence_note: No fitness-specific source was found. Safety or health claims are not evaluated by this framework.

product_marketing.label: Product Marketing

rules.rule: Jump straight into the value. Skip long intros and logo animations. Use both a strong visual and sound at the start.
Show the brand and the main message within the first five seconds.
Quick demos with captions, quick cuts and varied angles tend to beat static talking-head promos. TikTok suggests 21-34 seconds for most ads.
Would a viewer send this for the product's usefulness or fun, without feeling sold to?
Carry the message through both sound and on-screen text or visuals. Pairing speech with music is linked with better brand interest in Meta's playbook.
The CTA should feel like the obvious next step and be shown both visually and in the voiceover.

common_mistakes: Brand or message appears very late
Scripted, ad-like tone that does not feel native

general.label: General (fallback for any other topic, including food and recipe reels)
detect_hints: anything that does not fit the niches above

rules.rule: Be engaging from the first second. The opening should show or state what the video is about.
One main idea. Spoken content also visible as captions or text.
Watch time is a top ranking signal. Use the length the story needs. Instagram calls 15-60 seconds the sweet spot for most creative formats; YouTube says no length is inherently better.
Sends and likes per reach matter. Would a viewer send it to a specific person?
Include audio that fits the content, and make sure the message also reaches viewers with sound off. For food-style content, appetising close-ups plus clear voiceover or text are common.
If there is a CTA, put it in the video itself, as text or audio or both.

common_mistakes: Opening shot does not show what the video is about
